content: Cervicitis refers to the inflammation of the cervical tissues. It can be classified based on its cause, anatomical location, and duration, such as infectious or non-infectious, and acute, subacute, or chronic. The most common infectious causes are Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Differentiating cervicitis from other conditions like endometritis, salpingitis, vaginitis, and vulvovaginitis is essential, as these can also cause vaginal discharge and pelvic pain. Mucopurulent cervicitis is often asymptomatic, but some patients may experience abnormal vaginal discharge, painful sexual intercourse, or intermenstrual vaginal bleeding. Risk factors for developing cervicitis include high-risk sexual behavior, a history of sexually transmitted infections (STIs), early sexual activity, multiple sexual partners, low socioeconomic status, smoking, alcohol or drug use, and bacterial vaginosis. There is no single diagnostic test for cervicitis. Two key diagnostic signs are purulent or mucopurulent endocervical exudate visible in the endocervical canal or on a swab, and easily induced endocervical bleeding upon gentle swab passage through the cervical os. A finding of more than 10 white blood cells (WBCs) in vaginal fluid, in the absence of trichomoniasis, may indicate endocervical inflammation caused by C. trachomatis or N. gonorrhoeae. However, cultures are more accurate for diagnosing gonococcal cervicitis. Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) are highly sensitive for diagnosing trichomoniasis. If untreated, cervicitis can progress to pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), which may lead to infertility, particularly in chronic cases. Active herpes simplex virus (HSV) infections during the perinatal and neonatal periods can result in neonatal morbidity. Other complications of infectious cervicitis include chronic pelvic pain, ectopic pregnancy, spontaneous abortion, premature rupture of membranes, and preterm delivery. Treatment involves antimicrobial therapy targeting C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae. The recommended regimen is doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for seven days. Alternatively, azithromycin 1 g orally in a single dose can be used. Concomitant therapy for N. gonorrhoeae may also be required, using azithromycin, doxycycline, or a fluoroquinolone. Treating sexual partners is crucial to prevent reinfection. Follow-up after completing antimicrobial therapy is necessary to assess for microbial resistance. Cervicitis is caused by both infectious and non-infectious factors. The most common infectious agents are Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae, with Chlamydia being the leading cause. Less common infectious causes include Trichomonas vaginalis, herpes simplex virus (especially primary HSV-2 infection), and Mycoplasma genitalium. Non-infectious causes include intrauterine devices, contraceptive diaphragms, and allergic reactions to spermicides or latex condoms. Cervicitis is more prevalent in underserved communities and developing countries. It is also more common in HIV-positive women compared to those without HIV. Screening for infectious causes of cervicitis, such as Chlamydia and Gonorrhea, is recommended for sexually active women under 25 years of age, those over 25 at increased risk, and all pregnant women under 25 or at increased risk. Primary prevention involves avoiding risk factors like high-risk sexual behavior. Secondary prevention focuses on early diagnosis and treatment of STIs, particularly Chlamydia and Gonorrhea. There are no specific findings for cervicitis on imaging studies like X-rays, CT scans, or MRIs, and ultrasound is only helpful if complicated by PID. Surgical intervention is not necessary for managing cervicitis.
